doc.title: Toshiko Akiyoshi interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 17, 1999

chapter: Childhood in China and move to Japan
title: Western-style music education and starting piano
summary: School music was Western; she began piano at seven after hearing a girl play Mozart.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: I’ve been told that. It’s one of the hardest. What was your exposure to music before you moved to Japan?

Japanese. I don’t mean Japanese, I think it was from a major restoration time, which was about 120 or so years ago, when Japan adapted Western culture. The school system came from England. And parts of both came from France. And so everything in education was in Western style. So we — for music we never learned the Japanese music but it was an old western music.
So I wish — they had others too. For example my second sister studied Japanese traditional performing art and dancing. But that was after school.
When you moved to Japan, had you started on an instrument before then?

I started to play the piano in third grade when I was seven years old. And the reason was when I was seven, that a nine year old girl played Mozart’s [inaudible] you know the Sonata, the third movement, and I really felt I’d like to play just like that. So I asked my parents if I could take lessons for the piano, and that started. And I really loved the instrument. I think that’s really my instrument so to speak, when I play I feel very happy.
